judgment.summary: The crossword and both house ads pass. All ten clue sets teach a correct, honestly scoped AI mechanism in plain adult-beginner language, end in a concrete action or check the reader can actually take, and use Rewind Era references that clarify rather than decorate. Brand spellings are exact, action labels name real destinations, no banned wording (Play/Learn more/hype/deficit framing) appears, and Canadian spelling is correct throughout ("blank cheque"; "recognize" is the correct Canadian -ize form). The house ads are on-voice and internally consistent: the LIBRAiRY ad's link matches its own copy about "context," and the Mme CLAi-O ad's voicemail joke reinforces the reflection-not-prediction framing used in the CLAIO answer explanation. Remaining issues are minor and listed below; none misteaches, overclaims, or breaks voice.
objectiveDefects: Link-format inconsistency observable within the artifact: both PAIGE links use "/newsstand#ns-feature-desk-title" while every other internal link uses a ".html" path (e.g., "/library.html", "/newsstand-crossword.html", "/games/madame-claio.html"). Whether the extensionless route works cannot be verified from prose alone, but the inconsistency itself is objective.
qualityFindings: AGENTS and LOOPS share the identical after-solve label "Follow the agent loop"; for LOOPS a label naming loops or stopping points would better tell the reader what she gets, though both plausibly point to the same chapter-14 content.
The PAIGE clue set is the only one with no Rewind Era texture and the thinnest teaching payload (it is essentially a cross-promotion); acceptable in a ten-clue set, but it is the weakest entry.
SKILLS and GRAPH both link to chapter 15 with different labels ("reusable AI skills" vs "workflow graphs"); reasonable if the chapter covers both, but worth confirming the anchor serves each promise.

Uncertainty, not a defect: PAIGE as a character and "Useful this week" as a NewsStand column are not in the provided canon (which lists The Breaking, The Daily, The Weekly, The Tribune). The canon file scopes itself to listed names only and is not exhaustive, so I flag this for canon confirmation rather than failing it.
The grid answer is rendered CLAIO (unhyphenated, standard crossword-entry convention) while all visible prose correctly uses "Mme CLAi-O"; fine as-is, noted only for completeness.

Strong entries worth preserving verbatim: the Spice Girls MEMORY hint, the Groundhog Day LOOPS explanation with its stopping-point advice, and the GRAPH explanation's "does the route include your approval before sending" question — each reference does the required two jobs (familiar and mechanism-clarifying).
judgment.readerChange: A reader leaves with more than ten vocabulary words: each answer explanation converts the term into a checkable habit — ask which route the AI used for a number (TOOLS), review and prune what a product has saved (MEMORY), decide which agent actions need approval before it starts (AGENTS), confirm the current brief is actually visible to the AI (PROJECTS/CONTEXT), read what a skill actually instructs (SKILLS), trace whether a workflow sends without approval (GRAPH), and give agent loops a stopping point (LOOPS). The framing "looking things up is part of the fun" plus the closing note that this is "not a test of which AI subscriptions you own" removes the ambient shame an adult beginner brings to a quiz format, and every hint link routes to a named next step in the LIBRAiRY or town, so a stuck solver has a purposeful detour rather than a dead end.
judgment.voiceComparison: This reads as Ali writing LAiDIES within the crossword form. Like Episode 1, the jokes are load-bearing: the Spice Girls line teaches that memory persists whether or not you want it to, Groundhog Day carries the need for a stopping point, the mixtape sets up reusable know-how, and Mulder and Scully make \"agent\" concrete — each passes the two-jobs test. The plain-teaching rule holds: every explanation leads with the mechanic in the shortest true sentence, with the reference as garnish. Honest-limits language (\"not a guarantee of good judgment,\" \"in products that offer this feature,\" \"a reflection, not a prediction\") matches Episode 1's you-keep-your-judgment stance, and \"A goal is not a blank cheque\" is a genuinely Episode-1-calibre line. The register is a notch quieter than Episode 1's narrative exuberance — no Steve, no heroine — but that is correct for a puzzle surface; nothing here is beige, templated beyond the form's inherent repetition, or AI-explainer flavoured. It belongs beside Episode 1.
